cards.text: This song is from David, for the choirmaster, with stringed instruments. The note at the top tells us the moment: the Ziphites, people from the town of Ziph in Judah (Joshua 15:55), went to Saul, king of Israel, and said, “Is David not hiding among us?” I spent YEARS in a junk drawer and NOBODY came looking for me, but David can't even hide without the locals handing out DIRECTIONS!

cards.question: David's hiding, and the Ziphites are tipping off Saul. What does David do first in this song?

answers.text: He asks God to save him
He runs for the next town

cards.text: And David keeps knocking: “Hear my prayer, O God; listen to the words of my mouth.”

cards.question: David begs God to hear his prayer and listen to the words of his mouth. Why is he pleading like this?

answers.text: Ruthless men are out to take his life
His own family has turned against him
He has fallen sick and can't get up

cards.question: David says the ruthless men rising up against him have no regard for ___.

cards.text: Then comes the word Selah. And right after it, this song turns a corner.

cards.question: After the Selah, David says God has left him to face these ruthless men alone.

cards.text: Ruthless men are after his life, and David says, “Surely God is my helper; the Lord is the sustainer of my soul.” That's like the power going out and somebody calmly saying, “Relax, I know who's got the flashlight.”

cards.question: David calls the Lord the sustainer of his soul. What is David counting on God to do?

answers.text: Hold him up and keep him going
Make him famous across all Israel
Hand him the throne right away

cards.text: Now David turns to his enemies, and to who's going to deal with them.

cards.question: David says he'll pay his enemies back himself.

cards.text: David says of God, “He will reward my enemies with evil.” Then he prays, “In Your faithfulness, destroy them.”
Then David stops talking about his enemies and makes God a promise.

cards.question: David turns from his enemies to the LORD. What does he promise to do for Him?

answers.text: Sacrifice freely and praise His name
Build Him a house of cedar
Fast and pray for forty days

cards.question: Back at the start, David asked God to save him by His name. Now David says he'll praise the LORD's name because it is good.
David closes his song by giving the reason for his praise. What does he say God has done for him?

answers.text: Made him king over all Israel
Given him a city of his own

cards.question: In the last line, David says his eyes have looked in ___ on his foes.

findings.problem: David's first appearance doesn't say who he is. Saul gets 'king of Israel' and the Ziphites get 'people from the town of Ziph in Judah,' but David gets nothing.

rule.text: The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: The opening card says the song is from David and gives the Ziphite backstory, but it never says who David is speaking to. Without that, the baker doesn't know this is a prayer to God.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on.

findings.problem: The blank asks the baker to finish the wording of the line 'men with no regard for God.' The choices are God, the king and the law, and nothing in the earlier cards lets the baker reason out which one the psalm uses. It tests wording they haven't seen, not meaning.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The card retells verse 3 ('Ruthless men are after his life') along with verse 4, but it cites only Psalm 54:4.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: Papa Dorin's voice is mostly flat. Only cards 1 and 8 carry any humor. Cards 3, 6, 10, 12 and 13 read like plain narration or a pleasant dad, with no reaction, comparison or self-deprecation. These spots could hold a laugh without muddying a fact, such as David's back-to-back pleading in verse 2, or the turn after Selah.

rule.text: Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
